subject: Cognitive Science
title: Metaphor and Conceptual Structure
description: One-minute skill: Metaphor and Conceptual Structure.

hook.text: We say arguments are "demolished" and theories are "built." Ideas become buildings in our minds.

buildup.text: Lakoff and Johnson argued that metaphor isn't decoration—it's how we structure abstract thought.

discovery.text: Conceptual metaphors map physical experience onto abstract domains: time is a moving object.

twist.text: People primed with warmth rate strangers as friendlier. Physical and social warmth share circuits.

climax.text: Metaphors aren't just words—they literally shape how we reason, decide, and feel.

punchline.text: We think in metaphors we barely notice.

quiz.question: What did Lakoff and Johnson argue about metaphor?
options: Metaphors structure how we think, not just how we speak

details.summary: Lakoff and Johnson argued that metaphors are not just poetic decoration but fundamental to how we think. We understand abstract concepts through concrete metaphors: time is money, argument is war, life is a journey. These conceptual metaphors structure reasoning, language, and perception.
details.whyItMatters: Conceptual metaphor theory reveals that everyday thought is deeply metaphorical. The metaphors a culture uses shape how its members reason about abstract issues.
takeaways: Abstract concepts are understood through concrete metaphors
Metaphors structure reasoning, not just language
Cultural metaphors shape how people think about time and life

faq.question: What is a conceptual metaphor?
faq.answer: A conceptual metaphor maps structure from a concrete domain onto an abstract one. Understanding is grasping maps physical holding onto mental comprehension. These mappings are systematic: we spend time, waste time, and save time, all drawing from the time-is-money metaphor.

faq.question: Do different cultures use different metaphors?
faq.answer: Yes. English treats time as horizontal; Mandarin also uses vertical metaphors. Aymara speakers place the past in front because it is known and the future behind because it is unseen. These different metaphors correlate with different ways of reasoning about time.
